question: The National Memorial Day of the Exiles and Foibe (Giorno del Ricordo) once again turned the spotlight on the issue of Istrian Italians not having been able to return to their homes lost under the Rome Agreement of 3 July 1965, which saw Italy sell property to Yugoslavia without the consent of the legitimate owners, in exchange for a reduction in war damages.

Despite the UN conventions recognising the right of refugees to return to their homes, the agreement was renewed with Slovenia and Croatia without bringing it into line with EU law, which prohibits collective expulsions. Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
What measures does it intend to take to ensure respect for the property rights and right to return of Istrian Italians, in line with the principles of European and international law?

Does it consider it necessary to revise the agreements with Slovenia and Croatia so as to ensure that they comply with EU law, particularly regarding the ban on collective expulsions and the protection of refugees’ rights?

Will it support dialogue between Italy, Slovenia and Croatia to resolve the issue of the property of the Istrian Italians fairly and in accordance with the principles of international justice and legality?
answer: Article 17 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the Charter) provides that everyone has the right to own, use, dispose of and bequeath his or her lawfully acquired possessions. However, according to its Article 51(1), the provisions of the Charter are addressed to the Member States only when they are implementing EU law.

On the basis of the information provided, it does not appear that the matter referred to by the Honourable Member is related to the implementation of EU law. In the present case, it is thus for the concerned Member States to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected in accordance with their national law and international obligations.
